questions.text: The Gibbs phase rule is:
questions.detailed: $F=C-P+2$, where $F$ = degrees of freedom, $C$ = number of components, $P$ = number of phases. The $+2$ accounts for temperature and pressure. If pressure is fixed (condensed systems), the +1 form $F=C-P+1$ is used.

questions.text: For a condensed (solid/liquid) system at constant pressure, the phase rule becomes:
questions.detailed: When one variable (usually pressure) is fixed, the $+2$ becomes $+1$: $F=C-P+1$. This is the working form for most metallurgical phase diagrams drawn at 1 atm.

questions.text: At the triple point of pure water (three phases coexist), the number of degrees of freedom is:
questions.detailed: For one component and three phases: $F=C-P+2=1-3+2=0$. The triple point is *invariant* — a single fixed temperature and pressure.

questions.text: In a binary system at fixed pressure, how many degrees of freedom exist in a two-phase region?
questions.detailed: $F=C-P+1=2-2+1=1$. One degree of freedom remains (usually temperature): fixing $T$ fixes the compositions of both phases. In contrast, a binary three-phase (eutectic) invariant point has $F=0$.

questions.text: The Clapeyron equation for a phase boundary is:
questions.detailed: Equating chemical potentials along a phase boundary gives $\dfrac{dP}{dT}=\dfrac{\Delta H}{T\,\Delta V}$ (since $\Delta H=T\Delta S$). It applies to any phase transition — melting, vaporisation, sublimation, or solid-state transformations.

questions.text: The Clausius–Clapeyron equation for vaporisation (where the vapour is treated as an ideal gas and $V_{\text{gas}}\gg V_{\text{condensed}}$) takes the form:
questions.detailed: Substituting $\Delta V\approx RT/P$ into the Clapeyron equation gives $\dfrac{d\ln P}{dT}=\dfrac{\Delta H_{\text{vap}}}{RT^2}$, or $\dfrac{d\ln P}{d(1/T)}=-\dfrac{\Delta H_{\text{vap}}}{R}$ — a straight line of slope $-\Delta H/R$ on a $\ln P$ vs $1/T$ plot.

questions.text: Water has $\Delta H_{\text{vap}}\approx40{,}650\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$ and boils at $373\ \mathrm{K}$ (1 atm). Using the integrated Clausius–Clapeyron equation, the vapour pressure at $363\ \mathrm{K}$ is about:
questions.detailed: $\ln\!\frac{P_2}{P_1}=-\frac{\Delta H}{R}\left(\frac1{T_2}-\frac1{T_1}\right)=-\frac{40650}{8.314}\left(\frac1{363}-\frac1{373}\right)$. The bracket is $7.39\times10^{-5}$, giving $\ln(P_2/P_1)\approx-0.361$, so $P_2\approx1\times e^{-0.361}\approx0.70\ \mathrm{atm}$.

questions.text: A liquid has vapour pressures $100\ \mathrm{mmHg}$ at $300\ \mathrm{K}$ and $400\ \mathrm{mmHg}$ at $330\ \mathrm{K}$. Its $\Delta H_{\text{vap}}$ is about:
questions.detailed: $\ln(400/100)=-\dfrac{\Delta H}{R}\left(\dfrac1{330}-\dfrac1{300}\right)$. So $1.386=-\dfrac{\Delta H}{8.314}(-3.03\times10^{-4})$, giving $\Delta H=\dfrac{1.386\times8.314}{3.03\times10^{-4}}\approx38{,}000\ \mathrm{J}\approx38\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

questions.text: The melting (solid–liquid) boundary of water has a *negative* slope $dP/dT$ because:

options.label: a
options.text: Ice occupies a larger volume than liquid water, so $\Delta V_{\text{melting}}<0$

questions.detailed: $\dfrac{dP}{dT}=\dfrac{\Delta H}{T\Delta V}$. For water, melting contracts the system ($\Delta V<0$, since ice is less dense), so the slope is negative: increasing pressure lowers the melting point. For most metals $\Delta V>0$ and the slope is positive.

questions.text: The lever rule is used to determine:

options.label: a
options.text: The relative amounts (fractions) of two coexisting phases

questions.detailed: In a two-phase region, the tie-line connects the two phase compositions; the lever rule gives the mass fractions from the distances to the tie-line ends: $f_{\alpha}=\dfrac{x_{\beta}-x}{x_{\beta}-x_{\alpha}}$. It is a mass-balance (not a thermodynamic) result.

questions.text: In a binary eutectic system at the eutectic temperature, how many phases coexist and what is $F$ (at fixed pressure)?
questions.detailed: At the eutectic point three phases coexist ($\alpha$, $\beta$, liquid). With $C=2$ and $P=3$: $F=C-P+1=2-3+1=0$. The eutectic is an invariant point — fixed temperature and fixed compositions.

questions.text: For the sublimation of a solid, $\Delta H_{\text{sub}}=60{,}000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. Using $\ln(P_2/P_1)=-\dfrac{\Delta H}{R}\left(\dfrac1{T_2}-\dfrac1{T_1}\right)$, doubling from $P_1=1\ \mathrm{Pa}$ at $T_1=400\ \mathrm{K}$ to $P_2=2\ \mathrm{Pa}$ occurs at roughly:
questions.detailed: $\ln2=\dfrac{\Delta H}{R}\left(\dfrac1{T_1}-\dfrac1{T_2}\right)$. $0.693=\dfrac{60{,}000}{8.314}\left(\dfrac1{400}-\dfrac1{T_2}\right)=7217\left(0.0025-\dfrac1{T_2}\right)$. So $0.0025-\frac1{T_2}=9.6\times10^{-5}$, $\frac1{T_2}=0.002404$, $T_2\approx416\ \mathrm{K}$ — near 400 K, i.e. a small temperature rise raises $P$ appreciably.

questions.text: On a $\ln P$ vs $1/T$ plot for vaporisation, the slope equals:
questions.detailed: From $\ln P=-\dfrac{\Delta H_{\text{vap}}}{R}\cdot\dfrac1T+\text{const}$, a plot of $\ln P$ against $1/T$ is a straight line of slope $-\Delta H_{\text{vap}}/R$. Measuring the slope gives the enthalpy of vaporisation.

questions.text: Increasing the pressure on ice (which contracts on melting) will:
questions.detailed: Since $dP/dT<0$ for ice (because $\Delta V<0$), raising pressure moves the solid–liquid boundary to lower temperature, lowering the melting point. This is why ice melts under the pressure of a skate blade.

questions.text: Which of the following is an *invariant* point in a one-component system?

options.label: b
options.text: Any point on a sublimation curve

options.label: c
options.text: Any point on a vaporisation curve

options.label: d
options.text: Any point inside a single-phase region

questions.detailed: Only the triple point has $F=1-3+2=0$. Points on the two-phase curves have $F=1$ (they define a relation $P(T)$), and single-phase regions have $F=2$.

questions.text: On a typical binary eutectic phase diagram, the eutectic reaction on cooling is:
questions.detailed: The eutectic reaction is $L\to\alpha+\beta$: on cooling, the liquid transforms simultaneously into two solid phases. It is an invariant (isothermal) reaction, in contrast to a peritectic $L+\alpha\to\beta$.

questions.text: Which statements about the Clapeyron equation are correct?

statements.text: It applies to any phase equilibrium (melting, vaporisation, solid-state transformation).
Its sign depends on the sign of $\Delta V$.
It requires the two phases to be in equilibrium.

questions.detailed: All three hold. Clapeyron is general to any phase boundary (I); the pressure–temperature slope can be positive or negative depending on $\Delta V$ (II); and it is derived by equating chemical potentials, i.e. assuming equilibrium (III).

questions.text: Choose the correct option:
questions.assertion: Applying pressure to ice lowers its melting temperature.
questions.reason: The molar volume of ice is greater than that of liquid water.

options.label: a
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: b
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: c
options.text: A is true but R is false

options.label: d
options.text: A is false but R is true

questions.detailed: Ice is less dense than water, so $\Delta V_{\text{melting}}=V_{\text{liq}}-V_{\text{sol}}<0$. In $dP/dT=\Delta H/(T\Delta V)$, a negative $\Delta V$ makes $dP/dT<0$, so pressure lowers the melting point. R is the reason for A.

questions.text: For a solid-state transformation with $\Delta H=1{,}000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\Delta V=0.2\ \mathrm{cm^3\,mol^{-1}}$ at $500\ \mathrm{K}$, $dP/dT$ is approximately (1 J = 10 Pa·cm³):
questions.detailed: $dP/dT=\dfrac{\Delta H}{T\Delta V}=\dfrac{1000}{500\times0.2}=10\ \mathrm{J\,cm^{-3}K^{-1}}$. Convert: $10\ \mathrm{J\,cm^{-3}}=10\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{Pa}=10\ \mathrm{MPa}=100\ \mathrm{bar}$, so $dP/dT\approx100\ \mathrm{bar\,K^{-1}}$. (Solid transformations need large pressures because $\Delta V$ is tiny.)

questions.text: "At a two-phase equilibrium boundary of a one-component system, temperature and pressure are related, so fixing one fixes the other."
questions.detailed: True. On a phase boundary $F=1$, which means $T$ and $P$ are linked by $P(T)$; specifying one determines the other. Only at the triple point ($F=0$) is the state fully fixed.

questions.text: During the solidification of a binary alloy between the liquidus and solidus, the compositions of the liquid and solid:

options.label: a
options.text: Change continuously, following the two phase boundaries

options.label: b
options.text: Stay fixed at the overall composition

questions.detailed: The tie-line and its ends move as temperature falls: the liquid becomes richer in the lower-melting component and the solid composition follows the solidus. The lever rule gives their amounts. This segregation underlies coring in cast alloys (only removed by long homogenisation).

questions.text: At the normal boiling point of a liquid (1 atm), what is the value of $\Delta G$ for the vaporisation?
questions.detailed: At the boiling point, liquid and vapour are in equilibrium, so $\Delta G_{\text{vap}}=0$ and hence $\Delta H_{\text{vap}}=T_b\Delta S_{\text{vap}}$. This is the same equilibrium condition used in the Clapeyron equation.
